name: Secession (Wiener Secession)
overview: Artist-run exhibition house for contemporary art at Friedrichstrasse 12, Vienna (secession.at, "artist-run since 1897").

Founded on 3 April 1897 by Gustav Klimt, Koloman Moser, Josef Hoffmann, Joseph Maria Olbrich and others, in opposition to the Vienna Künstlerhaus. Klimt was the first president (Wikipedia). The association's official name is Vereinigung bildender Künstler*innen Wiener Secession.
Motto on the facade: "Der Zeit ihre Kunst. Der Kunst ihre Freiheit" (To every age its art, to art its freedom), removed in 1908 (secession.at).
funding_verdict: Secession: mixed: public support, a bank as main sponsor, and corporate partners

press_items.title: "Secession: Holub bietet Rücktritt an" (no date or author visible; the article names Barbara Holub as president since May 2006)
report on the election of Ramesch Daha (5 October 2021)

name: Bengal Foundation
overview: Non-profit cultural trust headquartered at Bengal Shilpalay in Dhanmondi, Dhaka, with programmes in visual art, music, film, crafts, publishing, theatre and education (Wikipedia, foundation website).
Founded in 1986 by the industrialist Abul Khair, known as Litu, to "promote and showcase Bangladeshi art on a larger platform"; he still chairs it (Wikipedia, Bengal Institute).

Bengal Shilpalay opened in 2000 with a solo show by Mohammad Kibria and reopened in April 2019 as a renovated, museum-like space with two exhibition halls; Khair said it would no longer run commercial operations and planned to show around 8,000 works from its own collection (The Daily Star, 8 April 2019).
funding_verdict: Bengal Foundation: family company money: a private trust funded by Abul Khair Litu's Bengal Group
wider_context: In July 2024 the Anti-Corruption Commission approved a charge sheet against Litu, chairman of Bengal Group Limited, for acquiring illegal assets of over Tk 903 million beyond his known income and concealing more than Tk 1.24 million in his asset declaration (The Financial Express, 12 July 2024).
The ACC case was filed on 23 April 2017, and on 1 November 2017 the ACC questioned him on charges including embezzlement of money from banks and tax dodging (The Financial Express).
The ACC also found illegal assets of Tk 25.26 million beyond the known income of his wife, Mahua Khair (The Financial Express).

In June 2007 a Dhaka court sent Litu, then Bengal Group chairman, to Dhaka Central Jail on 30 days' detention after a three-day remand that followed his arrest in the Gulshan area (The Daily Star, 9 June 2007).
These cases concern the foundation's founder, whose company pays for it.

name: Britto Arts Trust
overview: Artist-run non-profit collective at Green Road, Dhaka (33, 33/1 BDDL Green Mart, Space 208 to 210, first floor). It calls itself "the first artists' run non-profit collective in Bangladesh with a global reach" and a "non-commercial contemporary art environment" (Britto Arts Trust website).

Founded in 2002 by six founding trustees, all artists. The founders say the idea goes back to 2000 and that they started officially in 2002 (On Curating interview with Tayeba Begum Lipi and Mahbubur Rahman, in conversation with Anastasia Baka, Leilani Lynch and Anna Wälli).
"Britto" means circle in Bangla (Bad at Sports).
funding_verdict: Britto Arts Trust: artist-run non-profit: the trustees' own savings, a six-year grant, donations and project funding from institutions
wider_context: documenta fifteen opened on 18 June 2022; days later the mural "People's Justice" (2002) by Taring Padi drew condemnation from the German and Israeli governments over what they called antisemitic imagery, and was covered up and taken down. General director Sabine Schormann resigned on 17 July 2022. Findings released in January 2023 concluded that the exhibition "served as an echo chamber for Israel-related antisemitism and sometimes pure antisemitism" (Wikipedia).

The mural was by Taring Padi, another documenta fifteen participant. Britto Arts Trust is on Wikipedia's list of the exhibition's participants, and its project was shown at documenta Halle (Showcase).

press_items.title: Keeley Haftner, "Bad at Art Forum #8: Not Retweeting Documenta Fifteen" (28 June 2022)

name: Braemhuis (Renaat Braem Huis)
overview: Live-work house and studio of the modernist architect and planner Renaat Braem at Menegemlei 23 in Deurne, a district of Antwerp, in a residential neighbourhood; it is named for him (Herita).

Braem and his wife Elza Severin planned it from about 1950; he filed the building permit application in January 1955, the shell went up from February 1957 and the finishing ran into early 1958 (Onroerend Erfgoed inventory).
A brick facade hides a concrete skeleton; split levels inside, with stairs, panelling, parquet and built-in cupboards in wengé, oregon and limba wood (inventory).
funding_verdict: Braemhuis: public: given to the Flemish government in 1999 and opened by the heritage network Herita with the City of Antwerp

name: Constant (Association for Art and Media)
aliases: Constant Association for Art and Media
overview: Non-profit association for art, media and technology with an office at Rue du Fort 5A, Saint-Gilles, Brussels, and a studio at Chaussée de Jette 388, Koekelberg (Constant, "Contacts").

Founded in 1997; the association has been on the Belgian company register since 12 February 1997, and its registered names since 2003 are Constant Vereniging voor Kunst en Media and Constant association pour l'Art et les Médias (Crossroads Bank for Enterprises). Its 1997 statutes set out to support audiovisual media, film, video, electronic arts and software (Constant, "More about Constant").

Its focus widened to free software, feminisms, gender, copyright alternatives, science fiction and networked art; it describes itself as run by artists, designers, researchers and hackers working in Dutch, French and English (stated by Constant).
funding_verdict: Constant: publicly funded: Flemish, Francophone, Brussels and municipal authorities, with EU and foundation project grants

name: Horta Museum
overview: Museum in Victor Horta's former house (no. 25) and studio (no. 23) on Rue Américaine in Saint-Gilles, Brussels, with its reception, offices, archives, shop and temporary exhibition space in the neighbouring building at no. 27, built by Jules Brunfaut around 1903 to 1904 and renovated by the architects OZON (Cercle Guimard). Brussels Museums gives the address as Rue Américaine 27.
Horta built the house and studio from 1898 to 1901 and sold both in 1919 after spending most of the First World War in England and the United States (Cercle Guimard; Brussels Museums).

At the urging of a small group of Horta admirers, the commune of Saint-Gilles bought the house in 1961; house and studio were listed two years later, and the museum opened in 1969, which the Cercle Guimard calls the first museum in the world devoted from cellar to attic to one architect (Cercle Guimard).
funding_verdict: Horta Museum: mainly public: the commune of Saint-Gilles owns and runs it, with Brussels public bodies, the Fonds Baillet Latour and an unnamed patron behind the 2026 works

name: Villa Empain (Boghossian Foundation)
overview: Art centre in an Art Deco villa at Avenue Franklin Roosevelt 67, beside the Bois de la Cambre in Brussels (villaempain.com, Wikipedia).

Built from 1930 to 1934 by the architect Michel Polak for Baron Louis Empain. The Boghossian Foundation bought it in 2006 and opened it in 2010 as a centre of art and dialogue between Eastern and Western cultures (Wikipedia, villaempain.com).

Named for its client Louis Empain, son of the industrialist Édouard Empain. Louis gave it to the Belgian state in 1937, and it later served as a museum, a Soviet embassy and the headquarters of RTL (villaempain.com, Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Villa Empain (Boghossian Foundation): privately funded: a jeweller family's foundation bought, restored and runs the villa, with membership donors

name: KIOSK
overview: Contemporary art exhibition space at Louis Pasteurlaan 2 on Campus Bijloke in Ghent (KIOSK).

An initiative of the non-profit Kunstensite vzw and University College Ghent's School of Arts; the programme began in 2006 in a small glass pavilion (artlead). Kunstensite vzw has been on the Belgian company register since 30 May 2007 (Crossroads Bank for Enterprises).

Since 2010 it has occupied the former anatomical theatre of the Clinical and Polyclinic Institute, built in 1905 by the neo-Gothic architect Louis Cloquet; glass and metal structures sit behind the brick facades (artlead).
funding_verdict: KIOSK: public support: a university-college art school, the Flemish government and the City of Ghent (stated by KIOSK)

name: Festival International des Arts du Bénin (FInAB)
overview: Multidisciplinary arts festival held in Cotonou, with the 2025 edition also in Porto-Novo and Ouidah (Financial Afrik, 16 February 2025).
Initiated by Ulrich Adjovi, who says the idea came from Benin lacking a major festival like its neighbours. The project took nine months to launch (La Nation, Josué F. Mehouenou, 10 February 2026).

Organised by Empire Événementiel, a subsidiary of Groupe Empire, which Adjovi founded in 2012. The group describes itself as pan-African, in entertainment, events, media, nightclubs and hospitality, operating in Benin, Togo, Côte d'Ivoire, Burkina Faso, Congo and Nigeria (Journal du Cameroun, press release of 29 March 2024).
funding_verdict: Festival International des Arts du Bénin: privately organised with government and sponsor support: Groupe Empire, the Beninese state's arts fund (FDAC), MTN and Canal+ Impact

name: Espacio Cultural Patiño
overview: Cultural centre of the Patiño foundations in the Sopocachi neighbourhood of La Paz, in the Guayaquil building on Ecuador Street (Patiño foundation website).
Created by the Simón I. Patiño Foundation, it opened on 14 September 1984 in the Alameda building on El Prado Avenue and moved permanently to Ecuador Street in 1996 (Patiño foundation website).
Named for Simón I. Patiño, born 1 June 1860, died 20 April 1947 (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Espacio Cultural Patiño: funded by the Patiño family foundations in Bolivia and Geneva
wider_context: Source of the fortune: in 1894 Patiño took a deed to land near Llallagua in settlement of a $250 debt, located a tin vein there in 1900 and built control of the Catavi, Siglo XX, Uncia and Huanuni mines; in the 1940s he controlled the international tin market. The 1952 Bolivian Revolution confiscated the Patiño Mines (Wikipedia, Simón Iturri Patiño).

Catavi mine: Patiño acquired it in the 1900s. The camp kept its largely indigenous workforce "in rigidly segregated conditions", apart from the American managers, with housing, water, shops, transport and bathrooms divided (Wikipedia, Catavi mine).

Catavi massacre, 21 December 1942: about 7,000 miners had struck for five days for a 100% wage rise, and the military fired on a marching crowd for six hours. The official report listed 19 dead and 400 wounded; workers' estimates reached 400 dead. Families lived in company huts without running water or toilets (Wikipedia, Catavi massacre). The Catavi mine page calls it "Patiño's Catavi mine".
The centre belongs to foundations created by Patiño in 1931 and by his heirs in 1958, so the tin fortune is the origin of the money that pays for it.

name: Kiosko Galería
overview: Contemporary art gallery and international residency at Calle Arenales 315, Santa Cruz de la Sierra (address as given on its website; a 2014 interview gives Arenales 319).

Founded in 2006. Raquel Schwartz is its founding director (Delfina Foundation; El Deber interview, 28 December 2014). Its international contemporary art residency programme began in May 2007 (stated by the gallery).
Schwartz also founded the RSV Foundation, and the website describes Kiosko as a project of Fundación RSV. She is also founding director of Nube Gallery (Delfina Foundation).
funding_verdict: Kiosko Galería: privately run by its founder's foundation, with residents' fees

name: Botswana National Museum and Art Gallery
overview: National museum and art gallery in central Gaborone, near the Main Mall (Music in Africa).
Created in 1967 by an Act of Parliament and opened to the public in 1968. Also called the National Museum and Art Gallery (Wikipedia).
It includes the National Art Gallery and the Octagon Gallery, and since November 2007 has overseen the National Botanical Garden (Wikipedia).
funding_verdict: Botswana National Museum and Art Gallery: public: Government of Botswana

name: Capacete
overview: International artistic residency in the Glória neighbourhood of Rio de Janeiro, with the residency house at Rua Benjamin Constant 129 and the Criolense Kitchen Club at Rua Santo Amaro 33 (CAPACETE history page).
Conceived by the artist Helmut Batista in 1997 (CAPACETE history page), who is listed as its overall director. Rubens Takamine is artistic director.
Its own history page calls it the oldest residence promoting public programmes and cultural exchanges in Brazil.
funding_verdict: CAPACETE: FUNARTE, the Ministry of Culture and the Foreign Ministry of Brazil supported its 2013 Frankfurt exhibition

name: Pivô
overview: Independent non-profit contemporary art space in the Copan building, Avenida Ipiranga 200, loja 54, in central São Paulo. About 3,500 square metres at one end of the building (ArtReview, 2013; pivo.org.br).
Founded in 2011 and open to the public since 2012. Fernanda Brenner is the founder and artistic director (pivo.org.br). ArtReview (Claire Rigby, 2013) quotes her as co-founder.

Building: the Copan is an S-shaped Oscar Niemeyer building with about 5,000 residents. ArtReview (2013) says Pivô's interior had been empty for about 20 years before renovation, and that the space opened alongside the 2013 São Paulo Bienal with the show "Da Próxima Vez Eu Fazia Tudo Diferente."
funding_verdict: Pivô: mixed private: individual donors, galleries and an annual auction, with a tax-incentive scheme open to sponsors

press_items.title: Claire Rigby, feature on São Paulo (published online 2014, from the September 2013 issue)

name: Sofia City Art Gallery
overview: Municipal gallery of Bulgarian art at 1 General Gurko Street, Sofia, with its entrance from Knyaz Al. Batenberg Street (sghg.bg).

Began in 1928, when Mayor Vladimir Vazov decreed a commission to set up a municipal museum of Sofia with a museum, a library and an archive. A picture gallery was part of its work from the start (sghg.bg history).

Housing: various buildings from 1929. A purpose-built building opened in 1941 at 3 Banski Square and was destroyed in bombing. The gallery received its own space at 1 General Gurko Street in 1973, which opened in 1977. The library and archive separated in 1952 and the museum and the gallery became separate institutions (sghg.bg history).
funding_verdict: Sofia City Art Gallery: mainly public: Sofia Municipality

name: Laongo Granite Sculpture Symposium
overview: Open-air granite sculpture site and international symposium at Laongo, about 35 km from Ouagadougou (Wikipedia). The 2026 announcement places it in Bassitenga province, Wikipedia in Oubritenga province.
Founded by the Burkinabe sculptor Siriki Ky. The first edition opened on 13 January 1989 with 18 sculptors from 13 countries (Wikipedia). Ky is commissioner general of the 2026 edition (Sidwaya).
Named for the village of Laongo, where invited sculptors carve granite on site.
funding_verdict: Laongo Granite Sculpture Symposium: public: Burkina Faso's culture ministry
wider_context: Human Rights Watch, World Report 2026: the junta led by Ibrahim Traore cracked down on political opposition, the media and dissent. Unidentified men abducted the journalists Serge Oulon, Kalifara Séré and Adama Bayala, all critics of the junta, in June 2024; Séré and Bayala were freed in 2025 and Oulon is still missing. Authorities arrested three journalists in March 2025 and released them in July 2025.
The symposium is run by a ministry of that government and carries the president's patronage; the 2024 edition also featured the Alliance of Sahel States (Le360).

name: Sa Sa Art Projects
overview: Not-for-profit, artist-run space in Phnom Penh, on Street 350 since the White Building was demolished in 2017 (Cambodianess, 22 October 2022).

Established in 2010 by the Cambodian art collective Stiev Selapak, in response to the absence of a not-for-profit, artist-run space embracing diverse and experimental art practices. The co-founders include Khvay Samnang, Lim Sokchanlina and Vuth Lyno (Biennale of Sydney).

Began in an apartment in the White Building, a 1960s housing complex also called the Municipal Apartments, which housed municipal staff and then cultural workers and low-to-mid income families (Vuth Lyno, Afterall, 11 November 2020).
funding_verdict: Sa Sa Art Projects (Phnom Penh): donor-funded: a New Zealand-based foundation, benefit art auctions and project assistance
wider_context: documenta fifteen (2022) drew criticism in Germany. Taring Padi's mural People's Justice was condemned by the German and Israeli governments as antisemitic and was covered and removed days after the 18 June 2022 opening; general director Sabine Schormann resigned on 17 July 2022; an investigation released in January 2023 said the show "served as an echo chamber" for antisemitism (Wikipedia).

The criticism concerned the mural and the exhibition as a whole, not Sa Sa; Wikipedia lists Sa Sa Art Projects among the exhibition's participants and südostasien describes it as a guest at documenta fifteen.

name: Pitquhirnikkut Ilihautiniq / Kitikmeot Heritage Society (May Hakongak Cultural Centre)
overview: Inuinnait heritage and language society based in Cambridge Bay (Iqaluktuuttiaq), working to revive Inuinnaqtun, which it says has fewer than 500 speakers left (society website).

Incorporated on 6 March 1996 by librarian Kim Crockatt, Emily Angulalik, Ekvana Angulalik and Reverend Keith Todd, out of volunteer oral history and library projects begun in the early 1990s (2020-21 annual report). The name Pitquhirnikkut Ilihautiniq means "learning through culture".

The May Hakongak Community Library and Cultural Centre opened in May 2002 and is named for the local cultural advocate May Hakongak; it holds a public library, a museum space, an art gallery and regional archives (society website).
funding_verdict: Kitikmeot Heritage Society: mainly public: federal and Nunavut governments, with Inuit organisations, foundations and small donors

name: Great Northern Arts Festival
overview: Annual summer arts festival in Inuvik, a town of 2,500 or more people in the Beaufort Delta, on Inuvialuit and Gwich'in lands; its office is at Unit 301, 125 Mackenzie Road (festival website).
Run by the Great Northern Arts Society, founded in 1988 as a not-for-profit society; it calls the festival the longest standing pan-Arctic arts festival (festival website).

Began with an art show that Charlene Alexander and Sue Rose organised at the Inuvialuit Corporate Centre in 1989, bringing together about two dozen artists from Beaufort Delta communities (festival website).
funding_verdict: Great Northern Arts Festival: mainly public: Canadian Heritage and the Town of Inuvik, with Indigenous bodies and northern airlines

name: Dazibao
overview: Contemporary art centre and non-profit organisation at 5455 de Gaspé Avenue, suite 109, on the ground floor of the Pôle de Gaspé in the Mile End, Montreal (stated by the space; e-flux directory).

Founded and operating as an exhibition space since 1980, it was one of the first centres in Quebec and Canada devoted exclusively to photography, and has taken in the full range of image-based practices since the early 1990s (stated by the space).
It left 4001 Berri in 2009 for a two-year residency at the Cinémathèque québécoise, moved to the Pôle de Gaspé in 2014 and added a digital component in 2020 (stated by the space).
funding_verdict: Dazibao: public: Quebec, Canadian and Montreal arts councils and governments
